questions.question: A constant current source is supplying \(10\text{A}\) to a circuit shown in Figure. The switch S, which is initially closed for a sufficiently long time, is suddenly opened. Obtain the differential equation governing the behavior of the inductor current and hence obtain the complete time response of the inductor current. What is the energy stored in L, a long time after the switch is opened?
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Method 1
When the switch \(S\) is closed for a long time, the switch provides a short-circuit path across the network. Hence, the entire source current flows through the switch and no current flows through the inductor. Therefore, \[i_L(0^-)=0\] Since the current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously, \[i_L(0^+)=i_L(0^-)=0\] After the switch is opened, the source current divides between the resistor and the inductor. Applying KCL at the top node, \[i_L+i_R=10\] \[i_R=10-i_L \tag{1}\] Since the resistor and inductor are connected in parallel, \[v_R=v_L\] Using the element relations, \[Ri_R=L\frac{di_L}{dt}\] Substituting \[R=10\Omega, \qquad L=5~\text{H}\] \[10\,i_R = 5\frac{di_L}{dt}\] Using (1), \[10(10-i_L) = 5\frac{di_L}{dt}\] \[100-10i_L = 5\frac{di_L}{dt}\] \[\frac{di_L}{dt}+2i_L=20\] Hence, \[\tau=\frac{L}{R}=\frac{5}{10}=0.5~\text{s}\] The steady-state current is \[i_L(\infty)=10~\text{A}\] Using the standard first-order response, \[i_L(t)=i_L(\infty)+\Big[i_L(0^+)-i_L(\infty)\Big]e^{-t/\tau}\] Substituting \(i_L(0^+)=0\), \(i_L(\infty)=10~\text{A}\) and \(\tau=0.5~\text{s}\), \[i_L(t) = 10+(0-10)e^{-t/0.5}\] \[\boxed{i_L(t)=10\left(1-e^{-2t}\right)\ \text{A}}\] At steady state \((t\to\infty)\), \[i_L(\infty)=10~\text{A}\] The energy stored in the inductor is \[W_L=\frac{1}{2}Li_L^2\] Hence, \[W_L = \frac{1}{2}(5)(10)^2\] \[\boxed{W_L=250~\text{J}}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{Energy stored in the inductor after a long time }=250~\text{J}}\]
Method 2 (Using Source Transformation):
Transform the current source and parallel resistance into their Thevenin equivalent: \[V_{th}=IR=(10)(10)=100~\text{V}\] \[R_{th}=10~\Omega\] Thus, the circuit becomes, Since the switch was closed for a long time before \(t=0\), the inductor was short-circuited and hence \[i_L(0^-)=0\] Current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously, therefore \[i_L(0^+)=i_L(0^-)=0\] Applying KVL to the equivalent series \(RL\) circuit, \[V_{th}=R_{th}i_L+L\frac{di_L}{dt}\] Substituting the values, \[100=10i_L+5\frac{di_L}{dt}\] \[\frac{di_L}{dt}+2i_L=20\] Rest solution is same as Method 1.

questions.question: An \(11\text{ V}\) pulse of \(10\ \mu\text{s}\) duration is applied to the circuit shown in Figure. Assuming that the capacitor is completely discharged prior to applying the pulse, the peak value of the capacitor voltage is
questions.explanation:
Before solving, compare the pulse width with the circuit time constant. The equivalent resistance seen by the capacitor is \[R_{\text{eq}} = 1\,\text{k}\Omega \parallel 10\,\text{k}\Omega = \frac{1\times10}{1+10}\,\text{k}\Omega = \frac{10}{11}\,\text{k}\Omega\] Hence, \[\tau = R_{\text{eq}}C = \left(\frac{10}{11}\times10^3\right)(11\times10^{-9})\] \[\tau=10~\mu\text{s}\] The applied pulse width is \[t_p=10~\mu\text{s}\] Since \[t_p=\tau\]
Method 1
The capacitor does not get sufficient time to charge completely. Therefore, the peak capacitor voltage occurs at the end of the pulse \((t=10~\mu\text{s})\). Initially, \[V_C(0)=0\] At steady state, the capacitor behaves as an open circuit. Hence, using the voltage divider rule, \[V_C(\infty) = 11\left(\frac{10}{10+1}\right) = 10~\text{V}\] The capacitor charging equation is \[V_C(t) = V_C(\infty) + \big[V_C(0)-V_C(\infty)\big]e^{-t/\tau}\] Substituting the values, \[V_C(t) = 10+(0-10)e^{-t/(10\mu s)}\] \[V_C(t) = 10\left(1-e^{-t/(10\mu s)}\right)\] The peak voltage occurs at \[t=10~\mu\text{s}\] Therefore, \[V_{\text{peak}} = 10\left(1-e^{-1}\right)\] \[V_{\text{peak}} = 10(1-0.3679)\] \[V_{\text{peak}} = 6.32~\text{V}\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }6.32~\text{V}}\]
Method 2
Initially, \[V_C(0)=0\] At steady state, the capacitor behaves as an open circuit. Hence, using the voltage divider rule, \[V_C(\infty) = 11\left(\frac{10}{10+1}\right) = 10~\text{V}\] Since the capacitor is subjected to the input for exactly one time constant, by definition of time constant, the capacitor voltage reaches \(63.2\%\) of its total change. Therefore, \[V_C(\tau) = 63.2(\frac{10}{100})\] \[V_C(\tau) = 6.32~\text{V}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }6.32~\text{V}}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown in the Figure. If the frequency of the source is 50 Hz, then a value of \(t_0\) which results in a transient free response is
questions.explanation: When the switch is closed at \(t=t_0\), a certain voltage equal to \(\sin (\omega t_0)\) appears across the RL circuit at once, giving rise to transients.The transients eventually die out as the response reaches sinusoidal steady state. The expression for circuit current would be \[i(t)=ce^{-t/\tau}+\frac{V_m}{|Z|}sin(\omega t-\theta)\] where \(V_m=1\) and |Z| is the magnitude of circuit impedance. To determine the constant \(c\), we apply the initial condition at the switching instant \(t = t_{sub|0}\). Assuming the circuit is initially unenergized, the initial current at this exact moment is zero:\[i(t_{0}) = 0\] Substituting \(t = t_{0}\) into the current equation yields:\[0 = c e^{-t_{0}/\tau} + \frac{V_{m}}{|Z|}\sin(\omega t_{0} - \theta)\] By rearranging this equation, the arbitrary coefficient \(c\) is explicitly determined by the initial switching conditions:\[c = -\frac{V_{m}}{|Z|}\sin(\omega t_{0} - \theta)e^{t_{0}/\tau}\] To achieve a completely transient-free operation, we must entirely eliminate the decaying exponential transient term from the current expression. This requires the coefficient to vanish completely (\(c = 0\)).Therefore, the only way to satisfy \(c = 0\) is for the sinusoidal component to be zero:\[\sin(\omega t_{0} - \theta) = 0\] Hence, the condition for transient free switching requires: \[\omega t_0 = \theta\] Where \(\theta\) is the power factor impedance angle: \[\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega L}{R}\right)\] Given parameters from the problem: Frequency, \(f = 50\,\text{Hz}\) Angular frequency, \(\omega = 2\pi \times 50\,\text{rad/s}\) Inductance, \(L = 0.01\,\text{H}\) Resistance, \(R = 5\,\Omega\) Substituting these values into the condition equation: \[2\pi \times 50 t_0 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\pi \times 50 \times 0.01}{5}\right)\] Simplifying the term inside the inverse tangent function: \[2\pi \times 50 \times t_0 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right)\] \[100\pi \times t_0 = 0.561\,\text{rad}\] Solving for the switching time \(t_0\): \[t_0 = \frac{0.561}{100\pi}\] \[t_0 = 1.786 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}\] \[t_0 = 1.78\,\text{ms}\] \[\boxed{(B)\textit{1.78 ms}}\]

questions.question: An electrical network is fed by two ac sources, as shown in Figure. Given that \(Z_1=(1-j)\Omega\),\(Z_2=(1+j)\Omega\) and \(Z_L=(1-j0)\Omega\). Obtain the Thevenin equivalent circuit (Thevenin voltage and impedance) across terminals x and y, and determine current \(I_L\) through the load \(Z_L\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation: To find the Thevenin Voltage (\(V_{th}\)) we need to first open the load terminals. Let the Thevenin voltage be \(V_{th}\). Applying nodal analysis at node \(V_{th}\): \[\frac{V_{th} - V_1}{Z_1} + \frac{V_{th} - V_2}{Z_2} = 0\] Rearranging the expression to solve for \(V_{th}\): \[V_{th} = \frac{\left( \frac{V_1}{Z_1} + \frac{V_2}{Z_2} \right)}{\left( \frac{1}{Z_1} + \frac{1}{Z_2} \right)}\] Substituting the given values: V1 = \(30 \angle 45^\circ\,\text{V}\) V2 = \(30 \angle 45^\circ\,\text{V}\) Z1 = \((1 - j)\,\Omega\) Z2 = \((1 + j)\,\Omega\) \[V_{th} = \left( \frac{30 \angle 45^\circ}{1 - j} + \frac{30 \angle -45^\circ}{1 + j} \right) \times \frac{(1 - j)(1 + j)}{2}\] Evaluating the components: \[\frac{V_1}{Z_1} = \frac{30 \angle 45^\circ}{\sqrt{2} \angle -45^\circ} = \frac{30}{\sqrt{2}} \angle 90^\circ = j \frac{30}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[\frac{V_2}{Z_2} = \frac{30 \angle -45^\circ}{\sqrt{2} \angle 45^\circ} = \frac{30}{\sqrt{2}} \angle -90^\circ = j \frac{30}{\sqrt{2}}\] Adding the two terms: \[\frac{V_1}{Z_1} + \frac{V_2}{Z_2} = j \frac{30}{\sqrt{2}} - j \frac{30}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\,\text{A}\] Thus, the Thevenin voltage is: \[V_{th} = 0\,\text{V}\] To find the Thevenin Impedance (\(Z_{th}\)), we short circuit the independent voltage sources \(V_1\) and \(V_2\). Thus, \(Z_{th}\) is the parallel combination of \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\): \[Z_{th} = Z_1 \parallel Z_2\] \[Z_{th} = \frac{(1 - j)(1 + j)}{(1 - j) + (1 + j)}\] \[Z_{th} = \frac{1 - j^2}{2} = \frac{2}{2} = 1\,\Omega\] Since the open circuit Thevenin voltage \(V_{th}\) is \(0\,\text{V}\), the current flowing through the load resistance is: \[I_L = \frac{V_{th}}{Z_{th} + Z_L} = \frac{0}{1 + Z_L} = 0\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{V_{th}=0V, Z_{th}=1\Omega,I_L=0A}\]

questions.question: A series R-L-C circuit has \(R=50\Omega\), \(L=100\,\mu\text{H}\) and \(C=1\,\mu\text{F}\). The lower half power frequency of the circuit is
questions.explanation: For a series R L C circuit, the alternating current magnitude is defined by: \[I = \frac{V}{R + j(X_L - X_C)} = \frac{V}{R + j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)}\] Power dissipated in the circuit is proportional to the square of the current amplitude: \[P \propto I^2\] A half power frequency implies a frequency stage at which the current drops to \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of its maximum possible value. Maximum current occurs exactly at the circuit resonance frequency: \[I_{max} = \frac{V}{R}\] Given parameters from the problem system: \[\text{Resonant frequency},\,\omega_o = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = 10^5\,\text{rad/s}\] \[\text{Bandwidth},\,B = \frac{R}{L} = 50 \times 10^3\,\text{rad/s}\] Equating the current magnitude equation to the half power condition: \[\left| \frac{V}{R + j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)} \right| = \frac{V}{\sqrt{2}R}\] \[R^2 + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2 = 2R^2\] \[\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2 = R^2\] \[\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = \pm R\] Case 1: Considering the upper frequency branch where \(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = R\) \[\omega^2 LC - \omega RC - 1 = 0\] Dividing the expressions throughout by \(LC\): \[\omega^2 - \frac{\omega R}{L} - \frac{1}{LC} = 0\] \[\omega^2 - \omega B - \omega_o^2 = 0\] Solving this quadratic expression for the upper root \(\omega_1\): \[\omega_1 = \frac{B \pm \sqrt{B^2 + 4\omega_o^2}}{2} = \frac{B}{2} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{B}{2}\right)^2 + \omega_o^2}\] The second root is disregarded since a negative frequency \(\omega < 0\) is physically impossible. Case 2: Considering the lower frequency branch where \(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = -R\) \[\omega^2 LC + \omega RC - 1 = 0\] \[\omega^2 + \omega B - \omega_o^2 = 0\] Solving this quadratic expression for the lower root \(\omega_2\): \[\omega_2 = \frac{-B + \sqrt{B^2 + 4\omega_o^2}}{2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{B}{2}\right)^2 + \omega_o^2} - \frac{B}{2}\] The alternate solution here is also ignored because \(\omega < 0\) is not possible. Comparing both derivations clearly indicates that \(\omega_2 < \omega_1\). Substituting the operational data into the lower boundary frequency equation: \[\omega_2 = 19.258\,\text{krad/s}\] Converting the angular frequency down to cyclic linear frequency format: \[f_{low} = \frac{\omega_2}{2\pi} = 3.055\,\text{kHz}\] \[\boxed{(b) 3.055 kHz}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown in Figure, what value of C will cause a unity power factor at the ac source?
questions.explanation: Unity power factor implies that the overall network voltage and current are in phase, which corresponds to the condition of resonance. Thus, we need to make the imaginary part of the total impedance (or admittance) equal to zero. For this problem, since we have a parallel combination of elements, we calculate the equivalent admittance \(Y\) and set \(\text{Im}(Y) = 0\). The operational frequency parameters are: \[\omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 314\,\text{rad/s}\] The admittance of the capacitive branch \(Y_c\) is: \[Y_c = +j\omega C = +j314C\] The admittance of the inductive branch \(Y_l\) is derived from its branch impedance \(Z_l\): \[Y_l = \frac{1}{Z_l} = \frac{1}{30 \angle 40^\circ} = \frac{1}{30} \angle -40^\circ\] Converting \(Y_l\) into rectangular form: \[Y_l = \frac{1}{30} \left( \cos(-40^\circ) + j \sin(-40^\circ) \right) \approx 0.0255 - j0.0214\] The total equivalent network admittance \(Y\) is the sum of the parallel branch admittances: \[Y = Y_c + Y_l\] \[Y = j314C + 0.0255 - j0.0214\] \[Y = 0.0255 + j(314C - 0.0214)\] To satisfy the unity power factor resonance condition, set the imaginary component to zero: \[\text{Im}(Y) = 314C - 0.0214 = 0\] \[314C = 0.0214\] Solving for the required capacitance \(C\): \[C = \frac{0.0214}{314}\] \[C = 6.81 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{F}\] \[C = 68.1\,\mu\text{F}\] Wrapping the final calculated value to match standard rounding presentation: \[\boxed{(a)68.1\,\mu\text{F}}\]

questions.question: A two port network, shown in Figure is described by the following equations. \[I_1 = Y_{11}E_1 + Y_{12}E_2\] \[I_2 = Y_{21}E_1 + Y_{22}E_2\] The admittance parameters \(Y_{11},\,Y_{12},\,Y_{21},\,Y_{22}\) for the network shown are
questions.explanation:
Based on the provided circuit calculations, the admittance (\(Y\)) parameters of the given T-network (Y-form) can be found using two different methods.
Method 1
The given network is of the T-form consisting of three resistors of \(2\,\Omega\) each. First, we write down the open-circuit impedance (\(Z\)) parameters by inspection (Refer to Solution of Question 8.26.1): \[Z = \begin{bmatrix} Z_{11} & Z_{12} \\ Z_{21} & Z_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\] The short-circuit admittance (\(Y\)) parameters are obtained by taking the inverse of the \(Z\)-matrix (\(Y = Z^{-1}\)): \[Y = Z^{-1} = \frac{\text{adj}(Z)}{|Z|}\] The determinant of the \(Z\)-matrix is calculated as: \[|Z| = (4 \times 4) - (2 \times 2) = 16 - 4 = 12\] The adjoint of the \(Z\)-matrix is: \[\text{adj}(Z) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\] Therefore, the admittance parameters matrix is: \[Y = \frac{1}{12} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{6} \\ -\frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}\,\text{S}\] Thus, the individual admittance parameters are: \[Y_{11} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}, \quad Y_{12} = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}, \quad Y_{21} = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}, \quad Y_{22} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}\]
Method 2
Alternatively, we can directly convert the T-form (\(\text{Y}\)-network) into an equivalent \(\pi\)-form (\(\Delta\)-network). For a symmetrical T-network with equal resistors (\(R = 2\,\Omega\)), each resistor in the equivalent \(\Delta\)-network is calculated as: \[R_{\Delta} = \frac{(2 \times 2) + (2 \times 2) + (2 \times 2)}{2} = \frac{4 + 4 + 4}{2} = \frac{12}{2} = 6\,\Omega\] The resulting \(\pi\)-network has a series branch resistor of \(6\,\Omega\) and two shunt branch resistors of \(6\,\Omega\) each. By standard definition for a \(\pi\)-network with admittance elements \(Y_A\), \(Y_B\) (shunts) and \(Y_C\) (series) (Refer to Solution of Question 8.17.1): \[Y_{11} = Y_A + Y_C = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}\] \[Y_{22} = Y_B + Y_C = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}\] \[Y_{12} = Y_{21} = -Y_C = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}\] Writing the final \(Y\)-parameter matrix form: \[[Y] = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{6} \\ -\frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}\,\text{S}\]
Method 3
We can also find the \(y\)-parameters by shorting each port one by one. The y-parameter equations are : \[I_1=y_{11}V_1+y_{12}V_2\] \[I_2=y_{21}V_1+y_{22}V_2\] The \(y\)-parameters are defined as: \[y_{11} = \left. \frac{I_1}{E_1} \right|_{E_2 = 0}, \quad y_{12} = \left. \frac{I_1}{E_2} \right|_{E_1 = 0}, \quad y_{21} = \left. \frac{I_2}{E_1} \right|_{E_2 = 0}, \quad y_{22} = \left. \frac{I_2}{E_2} \right|_{E_1 = 0}\] Thus we need to investigate under two conditions : Case 1: Port 1 shorted (\(E_1 = 0\)) By applying the voltage division rule to find node voltage \(V\): \[V = \frac{2 \parallel 2}{(2 \parallel 2) + 2} E_2 = \frac{1}{1 + 2} E_2 = \frac{1}{3} E_2\] The current \(I_1\) is given by: \[I_1 = -\frac{V}{2} = -\frac{E_2 / 3}{2} = -\frac{E_2}{6}\] Therefore, the parameter \(y_{12}\) is: \[y_{12} = \left. \frac{I_1}{E_2} \right|_{E_1 = 0} = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}\] The current \(I_2\) is given by: \[I_2 = \frac{E_2 - V}{2} = \frac{E_2 - E_2 / 3}{2} = \frac{2 E_2}{6} = \frac{E_2}{3}\] Therefore, the parameter \(y_{22}\) is: \[y_{22} = \left. \frac{I_2}{E_2} \right|_{E_1 = 0} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}\] Case 2: Port 2 shorted (\(E_2 = 0\)) By applying the voltage division rule to find node voltage \(V'\): \[V' = \frac{2 \parallel 2}{(2 \parallel 2) + 2} E_1 = \frac{E_1}{3}\] The current \(I_1\) is given by: \[I_1 = \frac{E_1 - V'}{2} = \frac{2E_1}{6} = \frac{E_1}{3}\] Therefore, the parameter \(y_{11}\) is: \[y_{11} = \left. \frac{I_1}{E_1} \right|_{E_2 = 0} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}\] The current \(I_2\) is given by: \[I_2 = -\frac{V'}{2} = -\frac{E_1}{6}\] Therefore, the parameter \(y_{21}\) is: \[y_{21} = \left. \frac{I_2}{E_1} \right|_{E_2 = 0} = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}\] Thus, the calculated short-circuit admittance parameters are: \[y_{11} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}, \quad y_{12} = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}, \quad y_{21} = -\frac{1}{6}\,\text{S}, \quad y_{22} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{S}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • When finding the parameters from a \(\pi\)-network, do not forget the negative sign on the off-diagonal terms (\(Y_{12}\) and \(Y_{21}\)).
  • Ensure to convert resistance values (\(\Omega\)) to admittances (\(\text{S}\) or \(\mho\)) before computing matrix sum relations in the standard \(\pi\)-form.
\[\boxed{(b)\dfrac{1}{3}\,\textit{mho},\,-\dfrac{1}{6}\,\textit{mho},\,-\dfrac{1}{6}\,\textit{mho}\textit{ and }\dfrac{1}{3}\,\textit{mho}\textit{ respectively}}\]

questions.question: Let \(s(t)\) be the step response of a linear system with zero initial conditions; then the response of this system to an input \(u(t)\) is
questions.explanation:
Let \(s(t)\) denote the step response of a linear system with zero initial conditions. Then, \[s(t)=h(t)*u(t),\] where \(h(t)\) is the impulse response. The response of the system to the input \(u(t)\) is \[y(t)=h(t)*u(t).\] Since \[s(t)=h(t)*u(t),\] we have \[y(t)=s(t).\] Now, \[\frac{d}{dt}s(t)
=\frac{d}{dt}\left[\int_{0}^{t}s(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau\right],\] because convolution with the unit impulse is obtained by differentiating the convolution with the unit step: \[\frac{d}{dt}(s*u)=s*\delta=s.\] Hence, the required response is represented by \[\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\left[\int_{0}^{t}s(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau\right]}.\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }\frac{d}{dt}\left[\int_{0}^{t}s(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau\right]}\]

When the output voltage is \(V_{\text{o}} = +15\,\text{V}\), the non-inverting terminal voltage \(V_+\) is determined by superposition: \[V_{\text{UTP}} = 15 \times \frac{3\,\text{k}\Omega}{10\,\text{k}\Omega + 3\,\text{k}\Omega} + 2 \times \frac{10\,\text{k}\Omega}{10\,\text{k}\Omega + 3\,\text{k}\Omega}\] \[V_{\text{UTP}} = \frac{45 + 20}{13} = 5\,\text{V}\] When the output voltage is \(V_{\text{o}} = -15\,\text{V}\): \[V_{\text{LTP}} = -15 \times \frac{3}{13} + 2 \times \frac{10}{13} = -\frac{25}{13}\,\text{V}\] Since the input \(v_{\text{in}} = 10\sin(\omega t)\) is applied to the inverting terminal, the output switches from \(+15\,\text{V}\) to \(-15\,\text{V}\) when \(v_{\text{in}}\) exceeds \(V_{\text{UTP}} = 5\,\text{V}\). questions.question: Determine the transfer function \(\left(\dfrac{V_y}{V_x}\right)\) for the RC network shown in Fig.(a). This network is used as a feedback circuit in an oscillator circuit shown in Fig.(b) to generate sinusoidal oscillations. Assuming that the operational amplifier is ideal, determine \(R_{\text{F}}\) for generating these oscillations. Also, determine the oscillation frequency if \(R = 10\text{ k}\Omega\) and \(C = 100\text{ pF}\).
questions.explanation:
Applying Nodal Analysis at intermediate node \(V\): \[\frac{V - V_{\text{x}}}{R} + \frac{V - V_{\text{y}}}{\frac{1}{sC}} + \frac{V}{\frac{1}{sC}} = 0 \quad \text{--- (1)}\] By potential division for \(V_{\text{y}}\) from \(V\): \[V_{\text{y}} = V \left( \frac{R}{R + \frac{1}{sC}} \right) \implies V = V_{\text{y}} \left( \frac{1 + sCR}{sCR} \right)\] Substituting \(V\) into equation (1): \[\frac{V - V_{\text{x}}}{R} + (V - V_{\text{y}})sC + V sC = 0\] \[\left( \frac{1 + sCR}{sCR} \right)(1 + 2sCR) V_{\text{y}} = V_{\text{x}} + V_{\text{y}} sCR\] \[\frac{V_{\text{y}}}{V_{\text{x}}} = \frac{sCR}{1 + 3sCR + (sCR)^2}\] For frequency response, substitute \(s = j\omega\): \[\beta(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega CR}{1 - \omega^2 C^2 R^2 + j 3\omega CR}\] For sustained oscillations, the phase shift of \(\beta(j\omega)\) must be \(0^\circ\), so the imaginary part of the denominator must vanish: \[1 - \omega^2 C^2 R^2 = 0 \implies \omega = \frac{1}{RC}\] At the frequency of oscillation \(\omega\): \[\beta = \frac{j\omega CR}{j3\omega CR} = \frac{1}{3}\] Applying Barkhausen criterion (\(A\beta = 1\)): \[A = 1 + \frac{R_{\text{F}}}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = 3 \implies R_{\text{F}} = 2\,\text{k}\Omega\] Frequency of oscillation \(f\): \[f = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 10\,\text{k}\Omega \times 100\,\text{pF}} = 159.15\,\text{kHz}\] \[\boxed{2\,\text{k}\Omega, 159.15\,\text{kHz}}\]
Key points
Wien Bridge / RC Lead-Lag Oscillator: The feedback network provides a maximum feedback factor of \(\beta = 1/3\) with \(0^\circ\) phase shift at \(\omega_0 = 1/(RC)\), requiring a non-inverting amplifier gain of \(A = 3\).

questions.question: A unity feedback system has an open loop transfer function, \(G(s) = \dfrac{K}{s^2}\). The root locus plot is
questions.explanation: Given open-loop transfer function: \[G(s)H(s) = \frac{K}{s^2}\] The system has \(2\) open-loop poles located at the origin (\(s = 0, 0\)) and no open-loop zeros (\(Z = 0\)). The number of branches going to infinity is: \[P - Z = 2 - 0 = 2\] The centroid (\(\sigma_A\)) of the asymptotes is calculated as: \[\sigma_A = \frac{\sum \text{Real part of poles} - \sum \text{Real part of zeros}}{P - Z} = \frac{0 - 0}{2} = 0\] The angles of asymptotes (\(\phi_l\)) are given by: \[\phi_l = \frac{(2l + 1)180^\circ}{P - Z}, \quad \text{where } l = 0, 1\] \[\phi_0 = \frac{180^\circ}{2} = 90^\circ, \quad \phi_1 = \frac{3 \times 180^\circ}{2} = 270^\circ\] Thus, the two root locus branches emerge from the origin and travel vertically along the imaginary axis (\(j\omega\)-axis) towards infinity as \(K\) increases from \(0\) to \(\infty\). \[\boxed{\text{(B)}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The open loop transfer function of a unity feedback system is given by \(G(s) = \dfrac{2(s + \alpha)}{s(s + 2)(s + 10)}\). Sketch the root locus as \(\alpha\) varies from \(0\) to \(\infty\). Find the angle and real axis intercept of the asymptotes, breakaway points and the imaginary axis crossing points, if any.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given: \[G(s)=\frac{2(s+\alpha)}{s(s+2)(s+10)},\qquad H(s)=1\] Since the root locus is plotted with respect to the parameter \(\alpha\): \[1+G(s)H(s)=0 \implies 1+\frac{2(s+\alpha)}{s(s+2)(s+10)}=0 \implies s^3+12s^2+22s+2\alpha=0 \implies 1+\frac{2\alpha}{s^3+12s^2+22s}=0\] Hence, the modified open-loop transfer function is: \[G'(s)H'(s)=\frac{2\alpha}{s(s^2+12s+22)}\] Poles, Zeros, and Asymptotes: The modified system poles are: \[s=0,\quad s=\frac{-12\pm\sqrt{144-88}}{2}\] \[s=0,\,-2.26,\,-9.74\] Number of asymptotes \(A = P-Z = 3\). \[\theta_A=\frac{(2q+1)180^\circ}{3} = 60^\circ,\;180^\circ,\;300^\circ\] Centroid: \[\sigma_A=\frac{\sum p-\sum z}{P-Z}=\frac{-9.74-2.26}{3}=-4\] Breakaway Point: Isolating \(\alpha\) and setting \(\frac{d\alpha}{ds}=0\): \[\alpha=-\frac{s^3+12s^2+22s}{2} \implies 3s^2+24s+22=0\] \[s=\frac{-24\pm17.66}{6} \implies s=-1.05,\,-6.94\] Only \(s=-1.05\) lies on a valid root locus segment. Imaginary axis crossing point:
\[\begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 1 & 22\\ s^2 & 12 & 2\alpha\\ s^1 & \dfrac{264-2\alpha}{12} & 0\\ s^0 & 2\alpha & 0 \end{array}\] From the Routh array, for marginal stability: \[\frac{264-2\alpha}{12} = 0 \implies \alpha=132\] A.E: \(12s^2 + 2(132) = 0 \implies s=\pm j\,4.69\). img/ch5_root_locus/5_02_2.png
Mistakes to avoid
Do not use the original zero at \(s=-\alpha\) while computing asymptotes; the root locus rules must be applied to the modified open-loop transfer function where \(\alpha\) acts as the gain.

A dc series motor fed from rated supply voltage is overloaded and its magnetic circuit is saturated. The torque-speed characteristic of this motor will approximately be represented by which curve of Fig.3.02.1? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
When a DC series motor is overloaded, its magnetic circuit becomes saturated. Hence, flux becomes practically constant and is no longer proportional to field current. Since, \[T=k\phi I_a\] For constant flux, \[T=k_1I_a\] Also, \[\omega=\frac{E}{k\phi} =\frac{V-I_a(R_a+R_f)}{k_1}\] Using \(I_a=\dfrac{T}{k_1}\), \[\omega = -\frac{(R_a+R_f)}{k_1^2}T+\frac{V}{k_1}\] [figure unavailable] Thus, the speed-torque characteristic is a straight line with negative slope. \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • In saturation, flux becomes nearly constant.
  • For a DC series motor under saturation, \(T\propto I_a\).
  • Speed varies linearly and decreases with increase in torque.
  • The speed-torque characteristic has negative slope.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use \(\phi\propto I_a\) after saturation.
  • Do not assume \(T\propto I_a^2\) in the saturated region.
  • Remember that overloading causes flux saturation in a DC series motor.

Answer the questions Q\(3.06.1\) and Q\(3.06.2\) based on the data below A generator feeds power to an infinite bus through a double circuit transmission line. A Three-phase fault occurs at the middle point of one of the lines. The infinite bus voltage is \(1\) pu, the transient internal voltage of the generator is \(1.1\) pu and the equivalent transfer admittance during fault is \(0.8\) pu. The \(100\) MVA generator has an inertia constant of \(5\) MJ/MVA and was delivering \(1.0\) pu power prior to the fault with rotor power angle of \(30^\circ\). The system frequency is \(50\) Hz.

Consider a power system with three identical generators. The transmission losses are negligible. One generator (G1) has a speed governor which maintains its speed constant at the rated value, while the other generators (G2 and G3) have governors with a droop of \(5\%\). If the load of the system is increased, then in steady state,
options: generation of G2 and G3 is increased equally while generation of G1 is unchanged.
generation of G1 alone is increased while generation of G2 and G3 is unchanged.
generation of G1, G2 and G3 is increased equally.
generation of G1, G2 and G3 is increased in the ratio \(0.5:0.25:0.25\).
questions.explanation:
A generator operating in isochronous mode maintains the system frequency (speed) constant at its rated value. Generator \(G_1\) has a governor that maintains constant speed. Therefore, \[\Delta f = 0\] Generators \(G_2\) and \(G_3\) operate with a droop characteristic of \(5\%\). For a droop-controlled generator, \[\Delta P = -\frac{1}{R}\Delta f\] Since the system frequency does not change, \[\Delta f = 0\] hence, \[\Delta P_{G_2}=0\] and \[\Delta P_{G_3}=0\] Therefore, the increase in load is supplied entirely by generator \(G_1\). Considering negligible transmission losses, \[\Delta P_D = \Delta P_{G_1}\] Thus, generation of \(G_1\) alone increases while the generation of \(G_2\) and \(G_3\) remains unchanged. \[\boxed{\text{(B) generation of G1 alone is increased while generation of G2 and G3 is unchanged.}}\]
Key points
  • An isochronous governor maintains system frequency at the rated value.
  • A droop governor changes output only when frequency changes.
  • With \(\Delta f=0\), generators operating on droop characteristics do not change their power output.
  • Under negligible transmission losses, the additional load demand must be supplied by the isochronous machine.

Answer the questions Q\(3.06.1\) and Q\(3.06.2\) based on the data below A generator feeds power to an infinite bus through a double circuit transmission line. A Three-phase fault occurs at the middle point of one of the lines. The infinite bus voltage is \(1\) pu, the transient internal voltage of the generator is \(1.1\) pu and the equivalent transfer admittance during fault is \(0.8\) pu. The \(100\) MVA generator has an inertia constant of \(5\) MJ/MVA and was delivering \(1.0\) pu power prior to the fault with rotor power angle of \(30^\circ\). The system frequency is \(50\) Hz.

A synchronous generator is to be connected to an infinite bus through a transmission line of reactance \(X=0.2\) pu, as shown in figure below. The generator data is as follows:\[x' = 0.1\;\text{pu},\quad E' = 1.0\;\text{pu},\quad H = 5\;\text{MJ/MVA}\]\[P_m = 0.0\;\text{pu},\quad \omega_B = 2\pi\times50\;\text{rad/s}\] All quantities are expressed on a common base. The generator is initially running on open circuit with the frequency of the open-circuit voltage slightly higher than that of the infinite bus. If at the instant of switch closure\[\delta = 0 \ \text{and} \ \omega=\frac{d\delta}{dt}=\omega_{\text{init}}\]compute the maximum value of \(\omega_{\text{init}}\) so that the generator pulls into synchronism. Hint: Use the equation \[\int \left(\frac{2H}{\omega_B}\right)\omega\,d\omega + P_e\,d\delta = 0\]
questions.explanation:
\[P_e = \frac{EV}{X_{\text{eq}}}\sin\delta\] where \[X_{\text{eq}} = x'+X = 0.1+0.2 = 0.3\;\text{pu}\] Since \[E'=1.0\;\text{pu}\] and \[V=1.0\;\text{pu}\] \[P_e = \frac{1\times1}{0.3}\sin\delta = 3.333\sin\delta\] Given \[P_m=0\] the swing equation becomes \[\frac{2H}{\omega_B} \frac{d^2\delta}{dt^2} = -P_e\] Substituting, \[\frac{2\times5}{2\pi\times50} \frac{d^2\delta}{dt^2} = -3.333\sin\delta\] Using the given energy relation, \[\int \left( \frac{2H}{\omega_B} \right) \omega\,d\omega + \int P_e\,d\delta = 0\] Substituting \(P_e=3.333\sin\delta\), \[\frac{H}{\omega_B}\omega^2 = 3.333\cos\delta + C\] Applying the initial condition \[\delta=0, \qquad \omega=\omega_{\text{init}}\] gives \[\frac{H}{\omega_B} \omega^2 = 3.333\cos\delta + \frac{H}{\omega_B} \omega_{\text{init}}^2 - 3.333\] Hence, \[\omega^2 = \omega_{\text{init}}^2 + \frac{\omega_B}{H} \,3.333 (\cos\delta-1)\] For the machine to pull into synchronism, the limiting case occurs when \[\omega=0\] at \[\delta=\pi\] Therefore, \[0 = \omega_{\text{init}}^2 + \frac{\omega_B}{H} \,3.333 (-2)\] \[\omega_{\text{init}}^2 = \frac{2\times3.333\times\omega_B}{H}\] Substituting \[\omega_B = 2\pi\times50\] and \[H=5\] \[\omega_{\text{init}}^2 = \frac{2\times3.333\times2\pi\times50}{5}\] \[\omega_{\text{init}}^2 = 418.88\] \[\omega_{\text{init}} = 20.47\;\text{rad/s}\] Hence, the answer is \[\boxed{20.47\,\text{rad/s}}\]
Key points
  • After switch closure the machine behaves as a SMIB system.
  • Electrical power is given by \(P_e=\dfrac{EV}{X_{\text{eq}}}\sin\delta\).
  • Pull-in condition can be obtained using the energy integral form of the swing equation.
  • The critical initial speed corresponds to the limiting stable trajectory.

questions.question: A long wire composed of a smooth round conductor runs above and parallel to the ground (assumed to be a large conducting plane). A high voltage exists between the conductor and the ground. The maximum electric stress occurs at
options: the upper surface of the conductor
the lower surface of the conductor
midway between the conductor and ground
questions.explanation:
For a long conductor above a conducting ground plane, the electric field intensity varies inversely with the distance from the conductor. \[E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon r}\] where \[E \propto \frac{1}{r}\] Thus, the electric stress is maximum at the location where the distance from the conductor is minimum. Using the method of images, the conducting ground plane can be replaced by an image conductor carrying equal and opposite charge. The electric field lines become denser near the lower portion of the conductor facing the ground. Since the lower surface of the conductor is closest to the ground plane, the electric field intensity attains its maximum value there. Hence, the maximum electric stress occurs at the lower surface of the conductor. Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(B) the lower surface of the conductor}}\]
Key points
  • Electric stress is the electric field intensity at a point.
  • For a line charge, electric field varies inversely with radial distance, i.e., \(E \propto 1/r\).
  • The conducting ground plane increases field concentration on the side of the conductor facing the ground.
  • The method of images is commonly used to analyze conductor-ground configurations.

The input voltage given to a converter is \[v_i = 100\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t)\,\text{V}\] The current drawn by the converter is \[\begin{gathered} i_i=10\sqrt{2}\sin\left(100\pi t-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\\ +5\sqrt{2}\sin\left(300\pi t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\ +2\sqrt{2}\sin\left(500\pi t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\,\text{A} \end{gathered}\]

A three phase thyristor bridge rectifier is used in a HVDC link. The firing angle \(\alpha\) (as measured from the point of natural commutation) is constrained to lie between \(5^\circ\) and \(30^\circ\). If the dc side current and ac side voltage magnitudes are constant, which of the following statements is true (neglect harmonics in the ac side currents and commutation overlap in your analysis)
options: Reactive power absorbed by the rectifier is maximum when \(\alpha = 5^\circ\).
Reactive power absorbed by the rectifier is maximum when \(\alpha = 30^\circ\).
Reactive power absorbed by the rectifier is maximum when \(\alpha = 15^\circ\).
Reactive power absorbed by the rectifier is maximum when \(\alpha = 10^\circ\).
questions.explanation:
The displacement power factor is given by \[\cos\alpha\] Hence, the reactive power is \[Q\propto\tan\alpha\] As the firing angle \(\alpha\) increases, the reactive power drawn by the converter increases. Therefore, the reactive power is maximum when \[\alpha=30^\circ\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]
Key points
  • The displacement power factor of a line-commutated converter is \(\cos\alpha\).
  • Reactive power is proportional to \(\tan\alpha\).
  • Higher firing angle gives higher reactive power demand.

In the single phase diode bridge rectifier shown in figure 2.02.4, the load resistor is \(R = 50\,\Omega\). The source voltage is \(v=200 \sin(\omega t)\), where \(\omega=2\pi \times 50\) radians per second. The power dissipated in the load resistor R is [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: For a single-phase diode bridge rectifier with resistive load, the output voltage is the full-wave rectified form of the input voltage. Given, \[v=200\sin(\omega t)\] Therefore, \[V_m=200\,\text{V}\] The RMS value of the load voltage is \[V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}\] Power dissipated in the load resistor is \[P=\frac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R}\] \[P=\frac{\left(\frac{200}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2}{50}\] \[P=\frac{20000}{50}\] \[P=400\,\text{W}\] \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]

In the 3-phase inverter circuit shown, the load is balanced and the gating scheme is \(180^\circ\)-conduction mode. All the switching devices are ideal. [figure unavailable]

The figure shows an inverter circuit with a dc source voltage \(V_{\text{s}}\). The semiconductor switches of the inverter are operated in such a manner that the pole voltages \(v_{10}\) and \(v_{20}\) are as shown in Fig.Q4.02.1. What is the rms value of the pole-to-pole voltage \(v_{12}\)? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: The pole-to-pole voltage is obtained by subtracting the two pole voltages. \[V_{12} = V_{10}-V_{20}\] The corresponding pole-to-pole voltage waveform is shown below. [figure unavailable] The waveform has an amplitude of \(V_s\) and exists for a total duration of \[2\phi\] in one cycle of duration \[2\pi.\] Hence, the RMS value of the pole-to-pole voltage is \[\left(V_{12}\right)_{\mathrm{RMS}} = V_s \sqrt{\frac{2\phi}{2\pi}}\] \[= V_s \sqrt{\frac{\phi}{\pi}}\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{(B)\ V_s\sqrt{\dfrac{\phi}{\pi}}}\]

questions.question: The line-to-line voltage to the \(3\)-phase, \(50\,\text{Hz}\), AC circuit as shown in the following figure is \(100\,\text{V}\) rms. Assuming that the phase sequence is RYB, the wattmeters would read [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Given, \[V_L=100\,\text{V},\qquad Z=5\angle60^\circ\,\Omega\] Since the load is balanced and star connected, \[V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt3}=\frac{100}{\sqrt3}=57.7\,\text{V}\] Phase current: \[I_{ph}=\frac{V_{ph}}{|Z|}=\frac{57.7}{5}=11.54\,\text{A}\] Hence, \[I_L=I_{ph}=11.54\,\text{A}\] For the two-wattmeter method, \[W_1=V_LI_L\cos(30^\circ+\phi),\qquad
W_2=V_LI_L\cos(30^\circ-\phi)\] Here, \[\phi=60^\circ\] Thus, \[W_1=100\times11.54\cos90^\circ=0\] and \[W_2=100\times11.54\cos(-30^\circ)
=1154\times0.866\approx1000\,\text{W}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }W_1=0,\qquad W_2=1000\,\text{W}}\]

questions.question: Two in-phase, \(50\text{ Hz}\) sinusoidal waveform of unit amplitude are fed into channel 1 and channel 2 respectively of an oscilloscope. Assuming that the voltage scale, time scale and other settings are exactly the same for both the channels, what would be observed if the oscilloscope is operated in X-Y mode?
options: A straight line inclined at \(45^\circ\) with respect to the x-axis
questions.explanation: Given, \[V_x=\sin(\omega t),\qquad V_y=\sin(\omega t)\] Since the two signals are identical and in phase, \[V_y=V_x\] In X--Y mode, \[x=V_x,\qquad y=V_y\] Hence, \[y=x\] This is the equation of a straight line passing through the origin with slope \[m=1\] Therefore, \[\tan\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=45^\circ\] So the trace observed on the CRO screen is a straight line inclined at \(45^\circ\) to the X-axis. \[\boxed{\textbf{D. } \text{A straight line inclined at $45^\circ$ with respect to the x-axis}}\]
